pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — 10–11: solve problems that require answers to be ROUNDED to a specified degree of accuracy — rounding a computed (often decimal) result appropriately for the question or context.
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics, Y6): pupils 'solve problems which require answers to be rounded to specified degrees of accuracy' and 'determine, in the context of a problem, an appropriate degree of accuracy'.
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): builds on 5.NBT.4 (round decimals to any place) applied within 4.OA.3-style problem solving; SMP MP6 (attend to precision) frames choosing accuracy.
• Operational details — two intertwined skills: (i) rounding a result to a stated place (round 3.6875 to 1dp → 3.7), and (ii) deciding the SENSIBLE degree of accuracy from context, including cases where mathematical rounding must be overridden — money to the nearest penny, but 'how many containers hold the juice?' means rounding UP regardless of the digit (3.2 containers → 4). The child computes, then interprets: round conventionally, round up for 'enough', round down for 'how many complete', keep exact for money.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 10): compute a division and round to a specified decimal place. Tier B (10–11): choose the appropriate accuracy for a measurement/money context and round accordingly. Tier C (11): solve a problem where the unrounded decimal must be interpreted against context (whole containers needed → round up even though the digit says round down).
bestPractices: Distinguish ROUNDING RULES (nearest, by the following digit) from CONTEXTUAL rounding (round up for 'enough', down for 'complete whole units') — the classic buses/containers problems where the maths rule is deliberately overridden.
Round only at the END: teach children to keep full precision through a multi-step calculation and round the final answer, to avoid accumulated rounding error.
Use money and measures as the natural home: 'to the nearest penny' (2dp), 'to the nearest 10th of a second', so degree of accuracy is a real, purposeful decision.
Pair every rounded answer with the question 'does this level of accuracy make sense here?' — connecting to estimation/appropriate-accuracy (mt_ilPrU0cbtT) and to what the answer will be used for.
Rehearse the three context moves explicitly with sorting tasks: which problems round up, which round down, which round to nearest — so children choose the move by meaning, not habit.
keyRepresentations: Number line with the answer marked between the two candidate rounded values and the midpoint, to justify nearest-value rounding.
Context decision card: the problem, the raw answer, and a choice of round up / down / nearest with the reason.
Place-value view highlighting the digit being rounded and the deciding digit to its right.
Real-world icons (coins to the penny, containers that must be whole) anchoring why context overrides the plain rule.
commonMisconceptions: Applying the nearest-value rule when context demands rounding up ('need 3.2 buses' → answering 3 instead of 4) or down ('how many whole boxes fill' → rounding up wrongly).
Rounding at intermediate steps and accumulating error into the final answer.
Rounding to the wrong place, or using the wrong deciding digit (looking two places along).
Giving impossible precision for the context (money to 3dp, a count of people as a decimal).
Truncating (chopping digits) instead of rounding, e.g. 3.68 to 1dp given as 3.6.

learn.summary: For ages 10–11: solving problems whose answers must be rounded to a specified degree of accuracy, AND deciding the sensible degree of accuracy from context. Two intertwined skills: (i) rounding a computed result to a stated place using the deciding digit (e.g. 3.6875 to 1 d.p. → 3.7), and (ii) judging from the situation when the plain nearest-value rule must be overridden — round UP for 'how many are needed/enough' (3.2 containers → 4), round DOWN for 'how many complete whole units', keep to the penny for money, keep whole for counts of people. Keep full precision through multi-step work and round only at the end.

activities.title: Round it right: scenarios where the rounding move has consequences
feedback: If a child rounds to the nearest whole (5 buses), ask what happens to the extra 5 people; a 'how many are needed to fit everyone' question rounds UP whenever the division leaves any remainder, however small the decimal part.
If a child rounds a 'how many complete units' problem up, ask whether a partial unit actually counts as a completed one — if not, round DOWN.
When the child correctly rounds up to 6 even though the decimal (.33) is below .5, name the reasoning: 'you rounded by the meaning of the problem, not by the deciding digit.'
For 47 ÷ 6 = 7.833..., confirm the deciding digit (the second decimal, 3, which is below 5) sends 7.83 down to 7.8 at one decimal place.
activities.rationale: Choosing and seeing the consequence of a rounding move is intended to make contextual rounding concrete, which is the central judgement in this problem-solving objective rather than rule recitation.
sourceClaims: Y6 pupils solve problems which require answers to be rounded to specified degrees of accuracy and determine, in the context of a problem, an appropriate degree of accuracy.
Context can require rounding up ('enough') or down ('complete units') irrespective of the standard nearest-value rule, and answers should be rounded only at the end to avoid accumulated error.
learnerActions: Compute a problem that yields a raw decimal, e.g. 80 people needing 15-seat buses: 80 ÷ 15 = 5.33 (to 2 d.p.).
Choose a rounding move — round to the nearest whole, round down, or round up — and, where relevant, to which place.
Play out or describe the result of your choice in the situation: rounding to the nearest whole (5 buses) seats only 75 and leaves 5 people stranded at the kerb; rounding up to 6 buses seats everyone.
State in words why context (needing to carry everyone), not the deciding digit, forces rounding up here: the deciding digit (the 3 in 5.33) would round down to 5, yet the situation needs 6.
Repeat with a 'round down' context, e.g. 'How many complete 50 cm lengths can be cut from 3.4 m?' 340 ÷ 50 = 6.8 → 6 complete lengths, not 7, even though 6.8 is nearer to 7.
Repeat with a 'nearest' context where the plain rule does apply, e.g. 'round 47 ÷ 6 to one decimal place' → 7.8.
activities.intendedInsight: The context — what the answer is used for — decides whether you round up, down, or to the nearest, and this can override the mechanical nearest-value rule.

activities.title: Number-line rounder for the pure mechanic
feedback: If a child gives 3.68 to 1 d.p. as 3.6, point out they chopped rather than rounded: 3.68 is past the midpoint 3.65, so it rounds up to 3.7.
If a child looks two places along for the deciding digit, refocus them on the single digit immediately to the right of the rounding place.
For a borderline value with 5 in the deciding place, state the convention used (5 or more rounds up) and rehearse a few such cases.
activities.rationale: A visual number-line placement with the deciding digit highlighted supports the standard rounding mechanic and directly confronts truncation and wrong-place errors.
sourceClaims: Y6 pupils solve problems which require answers to be rounded to specified degrees of accuracy and determine, in the context of a problem, an appropriate degree of accuracy.
learnerActions: Mark the raw answer on a number line between the two candidate rounded values, with the midpoint shown.
Identify the digit being rounded and the deciding digit immediately to its right.
Decide which candidate the value is nearer to and round to it.
Deliberately contrast rounding with truncating: show that 3.68 to 1 d.p. is 3.7, NOT 3.6 (chopping).
activities.intendedInsight: Nearest-value rounding is justified by position on the number line and the single deciding digit; truncating (chopping digits) is a different, incorrect move.

activities.title: Money and measures: choosing a sensible degree of accuracy
feedback: If a child gives money to 3 d.p., ask what 0.001 of a pound would be in coins — there is no such coin, so round to the penny.
If a child reports a count of people as a decimal, ask how you could have part of a person; counts stay whole.
Praise reasoning that ties the chosen accuracy to how the answer is used.
activities.rationale: Money and measures give authentic reasons for choosing accuracy, making 'degree of accuracy' a real decision.
sourceClaims: Y6 pupils solve problems which require answers to be rounded to specified degrees of accuracy and determine, in the context of a problem, an appropriate degree of accuracy.
Pupils round decimals to any place and attend to precision, applying rounding within problem solving.
learnerActions: For a money result, round to the nearest penny (2 d.p.) and explain why 3 d.p. is not sensible for pounds and pence.
For a measurement context, round to the stated accuracy, e.g. nearest tenth of a second.
For a count of people, give a whole number and explain why a decimal count is impossible.
For each context, answer the question: 'Does this level of accuracy make sense here, and what will the answer be used for?'
activities.intendedInsight: The appropriate degree of accuracy is a purposeful decision set by the context and the use of the answer, not an arbitrary number of decimal places.

activities.title: Sort the problems: up, down, or nearest
feedback: If a child sorts by surface words rather than meaning, ask what the answer is being counted for.
Check that each sorting decision is matched by a stated reason, not just a category guess.
activities.rationale: Explicit sorting with reasons rehearses the three context moves and separates meaning-driven choice from reflex; on its own a sort checks classification rather than eliciting the full compute-then-interpret performance.
sourceClaims: Context can require rounding up ('enough') or down ('complete units') irrespective of the standard nearest-value rule, and answers should be rounded only at the end to avoid accumulated error.
learnerActions: Read a set of word problems and sort each into 'round up', 'round down', or 'round to nearest'.
For each, write the reason in words (e.g. 'need enough to fit everyone' → up; 'how many complete' → down; 'to the nearest tenth' → nearest).
Then solve two or three and carry out the move you sorted it into.
activities.intendedInsight: Children should choose the rounding move by the meaning of the problem, not by habit.

activities.title: Round at the end, not in the middle
feedback: If the two answers differ, ask the child to locate where the early rounding introduced the discrepancy.
Reinforce that the specified accuracy applies to the final answer, not to the working.
activities.rationale: Working the calculation both ways is intended to let the learner see accumulated error for themselves, which may motivate the 'round last' habit more concretely than simply being told it.
sourceClaims: Context can require rounding up ('enough') or down ('complete units') irrespective of the standard nearest-value rule, and answers should be rounded only at the end to avoid accumulated error.
learnerActions: Work a multi-step calculation twice: once rounding each intermediate value early, once keeping full precision and rounding only the final answer.
Compare the two final answers and describe whether and how early rounding changed the result (choose numbers where it does, so the effect is visible).
State the rule: keep precision through the steps, round last.
activities.intendedInsight: Rounding at intermediate steps can accumulate error; rounding only the final answer protects accuracy.

activities.title: Justify-the-accuracy discussion
feedback: If the child cannot explain why 5.2 coaches rounds up to 6, revisit that 0.2 of a coach still carries 10 people who need seats (0.2 × 50 = 10).
If the child says the answer never changes with re-wording, contrast 'coaches needed' (round up to 6) with 'nearest whole number' (5.2 → round to 5).
activities.rationale: Spoken Socratic reasoning targets the judgement aspect of choosing accuracy and surfaces whether the choice is understood or habitual; a discussion can prompt justification but does not by itself confirm the child can compute and round a fresh problem.
learnerActions: Given a real situation posed aloud, say whether you would round up, down, or to the nearest, and why, BEFORE the outcome is revealed.
Answer probing questions: 'Why round UP to 6 coaches even though 5.2 is nearer 5?'; 'If the question asked for the nearest whole number instead of coaches needed, would your answer change?'
Defend your chosen degree of accuracy in words.
activities.intendedInsight: Being able to justify the accuracy decision in context — and recognising that re-wording the question can change the correct move — shows command of the objective.

constraints: A sorting/categorisation or multiple-choice format can rehearse and check which rounding move fits, but on its own it does not require the learner to carry out the full compute-then-interpret problem or explain the reasoning — pair it with worked problems and justification.
A static number-line reference supports the rounding mechanic but does not let learners play out contextual consequences; use it alongside scenario and discussion work.
Treat animated scenario outcomes as one way to make consequences visible; the same insight can come from drawing, acting out, or discussing what happens to the extra people/units.
Distinguish arithmetic slips from rounding misconceptions: if the rounding logic is right but the division is wrong, have the child recompute and re-round rather than reteaching rounding.

Choose scenario numbers so the intended teaching point is genuine: to show context overriding the plain rule, a 'round up' context needs a fractional part below .5 (e.g. 5.33 → 6 needed), and a 'round down' context needs a fractional part of .5 or more (e.g. 6.8 → 6 complete lengths); otherwise the rule and the context agree and no override is demonstrated.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Self-audit of worked examples: 80 ÷ 15 = 5.333..., so nearest whole = 5 by the rule but 6 buses are needed — a clean rule-vs-context contrast now used in Activity 1. 47 ÷ 6 = 7.833... → 7.8 to 1 d.p. (correct). 260 ÷ 50 = 5.2 → 6 coaches (correct). 320 ÷ 50 = 6.4 → 6 complete lengths (correct). 3.6875 → 3.7 and 3.68 → 3.7 (not 3.6) (correct). The ORIGINAL row used 74 ÷ 15 = 4.93 for the override lesson, but 4.93 rounds up to 5 by the plain rule anyway, so it does not separate rule from context; the original 'close to 5 for a different reason' phrasing is muddled and was replaced.
The CCSS (5.NBT.4) and NCETM source claims are marked unverified in the original row; do not treat the mapping or the in-context rounding guidance as independently confirmed.
'Round half up' is stated as the convention; some curricula/contexts use round-half-to-even. Confirm the convention against the intended standard before teaching borderline (deciding-digit 5) cases.
Efficacy framing: activity rationales were softened to intended/may wording because these are unvalidated proposals; no empirical effectiveness or human review has been established.

probeDeeper: Why do you round UP to 6 coaches even though 5.2 is nearer 5?
To round 47 ÷ 6 to one decimal place, which digit decides whether you round up or down?
When is it right to round to the nearest, and when must you round up no matter what?
If the question asked for the nearest whole number instead of coaches needed, would your answer change?
assess.correctAnswer: 47 ÷ 6 = 7.83..., to 1 d.p. = 7.8. Coaches: 260 ÷ 50 = 5.2, but you need 6 coaches (the 0.2 of a coach still carries people, so round UP). The teacher watches for correct rounding-rule application AND context-driven rounding that overrides the rule when whole units are required.

errorPatterns.pattern: applies 'round to nearest' mechanically in the coaches context — 5.2 rounds to 5, stranding people
errorPatterns.nextMove: ask what happens to the extra 10 people; a real 'how many needed' context always rounds UP to fit everyone, regardless of the decimal.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: answer of 5 coaches; child rounds down because 5.2 is nearer 5

errorPatterns.pattern: rounds to the wrong place, or rounds the intermediate value too early distorting the result
errorPatterns.nextMove: round only the FINAL answer to the specified place; identify the digit that decides the rounding.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: answer given to the wrong decimal place, or rounded mid-calculation causing error

errorPatterns.pattern: uses the round-half-up rule inconsistently — unsure what to do with a 5 in the deciding place
errorPatterns.nextMove: state the convention (deciding digit 5 or more rounds up) and rehearse a few borderline cases.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: child hesitates or rounds 7.85-type values inconsistently

errorPatterns.pattern: rounds correctly, arithmetic slip in the division
errorPatterns.nextMove: do not reteach rounding; have the child recompute the division and re-round.

responseLevels.gap: rounds mechanically to nearest even in a 'how many needed' context (stranding people), or rounds to the wrong place.
responseLevels.full: rounds the final answer to a specified accuracy correctly AND rounds up/down as the context demands, explaining why the context governs the choice.
responseLevels.partial: applies the rounding rule correctly when asked for a decimal place but doesn't let context override it (or vice versa).

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Give the child problems where the rounding decision matters and watch how they round the RESULT: 'Work out 47 ÷ 6 and give the answer to one decimal place'; and a context one — '260 people travel in coaches holding 50 each. How many coaches are needed?' Watch whether they round by the rule when asked, but round UP for whole coaches regardless of the decimal.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The two items pull in opposite directions: one wants the rounding rule (7.83→7.8), the other wants rounding UP against the rule (5.2→6 coaches). A child who always applies 'round to nearest' answers 5 coaches and strands 10 people. Watching both reveals whether they let context govern accuracy — the objective's core.
